linkEnvelope.name: v2-live-full-envelope
linkEnvelope.note: A version 2 live-rendezvous link carrying every optional field at once: relay and ICE hints, a kith-gated policy, a pairing code (adding a device) and a room name.

linkEnvelope.name: v3-persistent-named-no-pairing-code
linkEnvelope.note: A version 3 stored group link: no pairing code, an open policy, and a name. Persistent invitations round-trip through the same envelope as v2, only the version number and the invitation.persistent flag differ.

linkEnvelope.name: v2-live-no-optional-fields
linkEnvelope.note: A version 2 link with none of the optional fields: no policy, no pairing code, no name. The fragment must carry none of their keys.

linkEnvelope.name: v1-legacy-secret-link
linkEnvelope.note: The version-1 shape from before invitations existed: the room traffic secret rides directly in the fragment (`s`), with no `j`/`h` invitation pair. `encodeRoomLink` writes this branch whenever `link.invitation` is absent, and a v1 URL carries no `v` key at all - `parseRoomLink` reads that absence the same way it reads `v: 1` would, which is the whole compatibility story for a link written before versioning existed.

linkEnvelope.name: v3-unknown-policy-tier-refused
linkEnvelope.note: A v3 (persistent) link naming an access tier outside open/ken/kith/kin is refused before the invitation itself is even read - a dropped rule would be an open room.

output.error: join URL carries an access policy at an unknown tier

linkEnvelope.name: v4-unsupported-version-refused
linkEnvelope.note: A link naming a version number this parser does not know (`v: 4`, one past the newest it understands): refused outright rather than guessed at as v1, v2 or v3.

output.error: join URL uses an unsupported version

linkEnvelope.name: bearer-31-bytes-refused
linkEnvelope.note: A bearer one byte short of the required 32: `roomInvitation` refuses it rather than accepting a link whose rendezvous derivation would not match what a correctly-sized bearer produces.

linkEnvelope.name: pairing-code-malformed-refused
linkEnvelope.note: A pairing code field that is not valid hex at all: refused with a named error, not an uncaught parse exception.

output.error: join URL carries a malformed pairing code

linkEnvelope.name: nine-relay-hints-refused
linkEnvelope.note: One more than MAX_RELAY_HINTS (8) relay hint: refused outright on encode, rather than silently keeping the first 8 and dropping the rest without saying so.

output.error: join URL carries too many relay hints

linkEnvelope.name: oversize-fragment-refused
linkEnvelope.note: A fragment one character past MAX_ROOM_LINK_FRAGMENT_LENGTH (16384): refused on length alone, before the fragment is treated as base64 or JSON at all.

output.error: join URL fragment is too large

linkEnvelope.name: hostile-input-normalised
linkEnvelope.note: A link nobody's own encoder produced: duplicate relay and ICE hints, a non-loopback ws:// relay (unsafe - the room requires wss:// off loopback), a loopback ws:// relay (safe - kept for local development and tests), and a name carrying a bidirectional override, a zero-width space and overlong text. `parseRoomLink` is still readable, and every hostile byte is normalised away rather than rejected outright: the invitation itself is genuine, only its envelope is adversarial.

linkEnvelope.name: quiet-room-without-members-refused
linkEnvelope.note: A policy asking for a quiet room (room.ts:83) but naming no members list: refused. A quiet room derives its per-pair keys from the members list, and with none there is nobody to derive them for.

output.error: join URL asks for a quiet room without a members list

linkEnvelope.name: unknown-agent-rule-refused
linkEnvelope.note: A policy naming an agent rule this reader does not know (room.ts:77): refused for the same reason an unknown tier is - dropping it would admit what the room meant to keep out.

output.error: join URL carries an access policy with an unknown agent rule

linkEnvelope.name: encoder-normalises-hostile-input
linkEnvelope.note: The real `encodeRoomLink` (link.ts:135-147) filters an unsafe ws:// relay, deduplicates the repeated one, drops an unrecognised ICE scheme, and sanitises an overlong/bidi-override/zero-width name - before the bytes ever reach a QR code, not only when a stranger's link is decoded. Fed the same kind of hostile input `hostile-input-normalised` (above) fakes directly on the wire; the output here is what the real encoder itself already wrote.

linkEnvelope.name: encoder-oversize-fragment-refused
linkEnvelope.note: 8 relay hints, each near the 2048 per-hint character ceiling, push the WRITTEN fragment past MAX_ROOM_LINK_FRAGMENT_LENGTH: refused at the point of encoding, not only on the way back in.

output.error: room link fragment is too large

invitationEnvelope.name: invitation-id-derivation
invitationEnvelope.note: The public rendezvous id: HKDF-SHA256 of the bearer alone. Pure - the real function is called directly.

invitationEnvelope.name: request-valid
invitationEnvelope.note: A request proving possession of the bearer, carrying an asking name and a participant pubkey. Built by calling the real `encodeInvitationRequest` with `crypto.getRandomValues` stubbed to the recorded [nonce, auxRand] queue - the NIP-44 nonce is drawn first (it is part of building `content`, which is evaluated before `finalizeEvent` signs), then the signature aux-rand.

invitationEnvelope.name: request-stale-refused
invitationEnvelope.note: The same request, read long after its 90-second window: refused as stale.

invitationEnvelope.name: request-device-mismatched-signer-refused
invitationEnvelope.note: M13: the event is genuinely signed by REQUESTER_A_SK - a real signature, not a zeroed or forged one - but the encrypted body claims a different device (`OTHER_INVITER`'s pubkey) than the key that actually signed it. `decodeInvitationRequest` checks `body.device` against `event.pubkey` and refuses the mismatch, or a stolen signing key could request admission in somebody else's device's name.

invitationEnvelope.name: grant-two-hop-delegation
invitationEnvelope.note: A grant signed by a delegated responder (not the root inviter), carrying the full two-hop chain rooted at the inviter. Both hops and both grant events are produced by calling the real `encodeInvitationGrant` twice - hop 1 by the creator, hop 2 by the responder hop 1 itself admitted - with `crypto.getRandomValues` stubbed to each call's own recorded 3-value queue: the new delegation hop's signature aux-rand (drawn inside the not-exported `issueInvitationDelegation`), then the grant body's NIP-44 nonce, then the outer event's signature aux-rand.

invitationEnvelope.name: delegation-chain-tampered-second-hop
invitationEnvelope.note: The two-hop chain above with hop 2's signature zeroed out. The whole chain is refused - a member cannot forge the last hop and admit themselves.

invitationEnvelope.name: delegation-hop-wrong-issuer-refused
invitationEnvelope.note: M5: hop 2 carries a genuine, validly-verifying schnorr signature - by IMPOSTOR_SK, a real keypair unrelated to this invitation - but IMPOSTOR is not hop 1's delegate (DELEGATE_A is). `verifyInvitationDelegation` walks the chain checking each hop's issuer against the PREVIOUS hop's delegate, so a validly-signed hop from the wrong signer is refused; only checking each hop's own signature in isolation would accept it.

invitationEnvelope.name: grant-signer-not-final-issuer-refused
invitationEnvelope.note: M9: the outer event is REALLY signed by IMPOSTOR_SK (a genuine schnorr signature that verifies), and the NIP-44 content REALLY decrypts under the requester's real conversation key with IMPOSTOR - but the delegation chain inside names DELEGATE_A as its final issuer. `decodeRoomAdmissionGrant` checks `body.delegation.at(-1).issuer` against `event.pubkey` and refuses the mismatch; without it, anybody could wrap somebody else's real, valid delegation chain in an event of their own and be believed.

invitationEnvelope.name: grant-secret-room-mismatch-refused
invitationEnvelope.note: M19: genuinely signed by the real root inviter, carrying the real hop-1 delegation chain (rooted and bound to fx.ROOM_SECRET_1's room) - but the sealed secret is fx.ROOM_SECRET_2's, a different room entirely. `decodeRoomAdmissionGrant` checks `body.delegation[0].room` against `deriveRoom(secret).roomId` and refuses the mismatch; without it, a chain authorised for one room could be reused to open a different one.

invitationEnvelope.name: grant-delegation-expired-refused
invitationEnvelope.note: M21: hop 1's real, validly-signed delegation names an expiry of 1800043170. Checked one second after that instant, the whole chain is refused - an expired hop is no hop, however good its signature.

invitationEnvelope.name: retirement-plain
invitationEnvelope.note: An ordinary retirement: the link was replaced, not the room ended. Built by calling the real `encodeInvitationRetirement`.

invitationEnvelope.name: retirement-room-ended
invitationEnvelope.note: A retirement that also says the room itself was ended, not just this link replaced.

invitationEnvelope.name: retirement-wrong-signer-refused
invitationEnvelope.note: A retirement signed by somebody other than the inviter pinned in the link: refused, even though the event itself verifies.

persistentInvitation.name: valid
persistentInvitation.note: A stored group invitation (kind 1463), published once and readable weeks later with nobody online. Built by calling the real `encodePersistentInvitation`.

persistentInvitation.name: tampered-ciphertext-refused
persistentInvitation.note: The valid event above with its final ciphertext bytes flipped: NIP-44's MAC check fails and the decoder must return null.

persistentInvitation.name: non-persistent-invitation-refused
persistentInvitation.note: The same event, decoded against the same bearer and inviter but without the `persistent` flag set: refused - a v2 (live) invitation must never be readable as a stored v3 group welcome.

persistentInvitation.name: room-mismatch-refused
persistentInvitation.note: M20: genuinely signed by the real inviter, genuinely encrypted under the real welcome key - but the body's `room` field (fcdc853ddc1be7f7d978367e1a5156b55f11e4c22a49db949f5bb939a303762a) does not match what its own sealed secret derives to (2848bdd5c60a79e2dfe667ae9616c1107f61709032b66e556e28f4a96e69450b). `decodePersistentInvitation` checks `deriveRoom(secret).roomId === body.room` and refuses the mismatch.

persistentInvitation.name: wrong-signer-refused
persistentInvitation.note: N7: genuinely signed and genuinely encrypted (the SAME bearer as INVITATION_3, so the same welcome key and `d` tag) - but by OTHER_INVITER_SK rather than the pinned inviter. `decodePersistentInvitation` (persistent-invitation.ts:49) checks `event.pubkey === invitation.inviter` and refuses: holding the bearer is not authority to publish as the inviter.

epochGrant.name: grant-with-secret-at-epoch-1
epochGrant.note: The authority answers a caught-up request: the room has moved to epoch 1, and the secret that opens it is sealed to the asking device. Built by calling the real `encodeEpochGrant`.

epochGrant.name: grant-wrong-request-id-refused
epochGrant.note: The same event, but the device asked with a different request id than the one the grant answers: refused.

epochGrant.name: grant-stale-refused
epochGrant.note: M18: the same genuinely-signed, genuinely-sealed grant, read 91 seconds after it was made (one past the 90-second window `decodeEpochGrant` allows): refused as stale, the same freshness rule `decodeInvitationRequest` applies.

epochGrant.name: grant-epoch-zero-no-secret
epochGrant.note: A grant answering "the room is still at epoch 0": no secret rides in the body, because the epoch-0 room key is already what the link handed out.

epochGrant.name: grant-refused-removed
epochGrant.note: The authority refuses the epoch request because the device's participant was removed from the room. Sealed like an ordinary grant, so only the asking device learns why.

epochGrant.name: grant-refused-closed
epochGrant.note: The authority refuses the epoch request because the device's participant was the room has been closed. Sealed like an ordinary grant, so only the asking device learns why.

epochGrant.name: grant-wrong-authority-signer-refused
epochGrant.note: M6: a grant genuinely signed and genuinely sealed by IMPOSTOR_SK - a real keypair, not the room authority. `decodeEpochGrant` checks `event.pubkey` against the caller-supplied `authority` and refuses before decryption is even attempted; holding a valid signature over SOME key is not holding authority over this room.

epochGrant.name: grant-wrong-room-refused
epochGrant.note: M18: a genuinely-signed grant whose `d` tag names a different room (fcdc853ddc1be7f7d978367e1a5156b55f11e4c22a49db949f5bb939a303762a) than the one being asked about (2848bdd5c60a79e2dfe667ae9616c1107f61709032b66e556e28f4a96e69450b). Refused on the tag alone, before decryption.

epochGrant.name: epoch-1-id-independent-check
epochGrant.note: `deriveEpoch` for epoch 1 from EPOCH_SECRET_1, called directly (pure, no signing) - confirms the secret sealed in `grant-with-secret-at-epoch-1` really does derive to that epoch's id and key.

epochGrant.name: grant-epoch-above-max-refused
epochGrant.note: Genuinely signed and genuinely sealed by the real authority key, naming epoch 1000001 - one past MAX_EPOCH (1000000). The real `encodeEpochGrant` refuses to build this itself (`requireEpochNumber` throws at encode time), so this pins the decode-side bound (epoch.ts:571) directly: an authority that was tricked, or a second implementation with a looser encoder, must still be refused on read.

epochGrant.name: rekey-epoch-tag-zero-refused
epochGrant.note: Genuinely signed and sealed by the real `encodeRekeyEvent`, called with a `current` naming epoch -1 (a value the real epoch-following path never holds, but that `encodeRekeyEvent` itself does not refuse) so that `next.epoch` (0) satisfies its `current.epoch + 1` check. Epoch 0 is the room's own secret, byte-identical to before any rekey, and is never itself announced by a rekey event. `peekRekeyEvent`'s regex (`/^[1-9][0-9]{0,6}$/`) refuses a leading zero outright, before the signature is even checked.

epochGrant.name: rekey-epoch-tag-leading-zero-refused
epochGrant.note: Genuinely signed by the real authority key, `epoch` tag the literal string "01". No real `encodeRekeyEvent` call writes this (`String(epoch)` never carries a leading zero for a non-negative integer), so this is hand-built. Refused by the regex's `^[1-9]` requirement - a leading-zero-tolerant regex, or an unanchored one, would wrongly accept it.

epochGrant.name: rekey-epoch-tag-above-max-refused
epochGrant.note: Genuinely signed by the real authority key, `epoch` tag "1000001" - one past MAX_EPOCH (1000000), and a shape (7 digits, no leading zero) the regex alone accepts. Hand-built because the real `encodeRekeyEvent` refuses to build an epoch this large itself. Refused by the separate epoch.ts:260 bound, independent of the regex.

epochRequest.name: credential-device-not-signer-refused
epochRequest.note: N2: the outer event is genuinely signed by KEPT_DEVICE_SK, and the embedded credential is genuinely signed by PARTICIPANT_A_SK and genuinely names REMOVED_DEVICE. Refused by TWO independent checks: the device check (epoch.ts:457) and the admission proof, which `encodeEpochRequest` always binds to its own real signer and so also disagrees with REMOVED_DEVICE. See `credential-device-not-signer-refused-admission-matches` below for a vector that isolates the device check alone.

epochRequest.name: credential-device-not-signer-refused-admission-matches
epochRequest.note: N2 (isolated): the SAME credential-device mismatch as above, but the admission proof is hand-computed to match REMOVED_DEVICE (the credential's claim) rather than the real signer - so the admission check alone would pass this. Only `decodeEpochRequest`'s device check (epoch.ts:457) refuses it. Genuinely signed and genuinely encrypted throughout; only the admission field is deliberately built to defeat the OTHER check, isolating this one.

personCredential.name: valid-accepted-with-acceptPerson
personCredential.note: A person-scope credential (device authorised for every room, not one) is refused as a room credential by default, and accepted only when the caller opts in with `acceptPerson`. Built by calling the real, async `createDeviceCredential` with an injected `ParticipantIdentity` whose `signEvent` is `finalizeDeterministic` under the recorded aux-rand.

asRoomWithoutAcceptPerson.reason: person credential where a room credential was expected

personCredential.name: valid-at-exactly-30-day-boundary
personCredential.note: M15 (accepted side): expiresAt is exactly 2592000 seconds (30 days) past createdAt - the boundary itself. Both `createDeviceCredential` (mint time) and `verifyDeviceCredential` (read time) use a strict `>`, so this is accepted; past the boundary ("refused-over-30-days" below) is refused. Minted through the real, async `createDeviceCredential`.

personCredential.name: refused-over-30-days
personCredential.note: M15 (refused side); updated for forgesworn/kithmoot#205: the real createDeviceCredential now measures the same way verifyDeviceCredential does - against the SIGNED created_at, not the requested now - and throws RestampedCredentialExpiryError at mint time instead of returning a credential. output.event/output.result keep M15's original coverage: the exact over-cap event a pre-#205 mint would have returned (built deterministically, the same bytes as before), and verifyDeviceCredential's own refusal of it, which is unchanged by #205 (its measurement was already correct - only the mint side was checking the wrong clock).

output.mintThrew: the signer restamped created_at, and the requested expiry now runs longer than 30 days from it

personCredential.name: wrong-person-identity-path-refused
personCredential.note: N9: genuinely signed by PARTICIPANT_B_SK, but its `d` tag names PARTICIPANT_A - claiming to be a device credential for someone else while signing with your own key. Checked via the `identity` path (credential.ts:136): refused, because `d` must equal BOTH the identity asked for AND the credential's own real signer - checking only the first half would accept this.

personCredential.name: wrong-person-acceptperson-path-refused
personCredential.note: N9b: the SAME event, checked via the room-credential-with-acceptPerson path instead (credential.ts:139): refused for the same reason - `d` (PARTICIPANT_A) does not match the real signer (PARTICIPANT_B), and this path checks nothing else about `d`.

channelsSignature.name: valid-at-epoch-1
channelsSignature.note: The authority signs the room's channel list at epoch 1. Canonicalised (deduplicated, sorted) before signing, and verified with the real `verifyChannels`, in either list order. Built by calling the real `signChannels` with `crypto.getRandomValues` stubbed to the recorded aux-rand.

channelsSignature.name: refused-at-another-epoch
channelsSignature.note: The same signature, checked against epoch 2 instead of the epoch it was made for: refused - a channel list valid at one epoch is not replayable into the next.

channelsSignature.name: refused-wrong-authority
channelsSignature.note: The same genuinely-signed message, checked against a different (real) pubkey than the one that actually signed it: refused. A member who holds the room key cannot present somebody else's signed channel list as if the authority had signed it for them.

channelsSignature.name: refused-wrong-room
channelsSignature.note: The same genuinely-signed message, checked against a different room's id: refused. A channel list signed for one room is not replayable into another, even under the same authority and epoch number.

channelsSignature.name: refused-reserved-channel-name
channelsSignature.note: `agents`, `minutes` and `transcript` are reserved: the room already means something else by them, so `canonicalChannels` throws rather than letting them into a signed registry.

accessEvaluation.name: kindred-proof-names-another-participant-refused
accessEvaluation.note: N11: a real, validly-signed kindred proof for GUEST, checked against PARTICIPANT_A instead. `evaluateAccess` (access.ts:96) refuses before it ever reaches the signature check - a proof is a grant to the one participant it names, not a bearer token any holder can present.

accessEvaluation.name: kindred-proof-expiry-at-boundary-refused
accessEvaluation.note: N10 (refused side): a real kindred proof checked at exactly its own `expiresAt`: refused. Proves the check is `<=`, not `<` - a boundary shifted by one would accept this.

accessEvaluation.name: kindred-proof-one-second-before-expiry-accepted
accessEvaluation.note: N10 (accepted side): the SAME proof, checked one second before its own `expiresAt`: accepted. Together with the refused-side vector above, this pins the boundary exactly, in both directions.

accessEvaluation.name: device-credential-expiry-at-boundary-refused
accessEvaluation.note: N8 (refused side): a real room-scope device credential checked at exactly its own `expiration`: refused (credential.ts:155, the same `<=` rule the kindred proof uses).

accessEvaluation.name: device-credential-one-second-before-expiry-accepted
accessEvaluation.note: N8 (accepted side): the SAME credential, checked one second before its own `expiration`: accepted.
